questions.question_text:
Consider $f(x) = \begin{cases} x^{2} + 3, & x \le 1 \\ 6x - 2, & x > 1 \end{cases}$.
Which statement about $f(x)$ at $x = 1$ is correct?

options.text: $f(x)$ is continuous at $x = 1$ but not differentiable there, because the one-sided gradients $2$ and $6$ are different.
$f(x)$ is differentiable at $x = 1$, because the two branches take the same value there.
options.why: Treats continuity as sufficient for differentiability; the implication only runs the other way.

options.text: $f(x)$ is neither continuous nor differentiable at $x = 1$, because the two branches have different rules.
options.why: Assumes a change of rule must create a jump, instead of evaluating both branches at $x = 1$.

options.text: $f(x)$ is differentiable at $x = 1$, because both $x^{2} + 3$ and $6x - 2$ are differentiable functions.
options.why: Checks that each branch is smooth on its own, rather than testing the gradients at the join.

questions.solution_text:
Let $g(x) = x^{2} + 3$ and $h(x) = 6x - 2$
$g(1) = 1^{2} + 3 = 4$
$h(1) = 6(1) - 2 = 4$
The values agree, so $f(x)$ is continuous at $x = 1$.
$g'(x) = 2x$, so $g'(1) = 2$
$h'(x) = 6$, so $h'(1) = 6$
The gradients differ, so $f(x)$ is continuous but not differentiable at $x = 1$.

questions.question_text: State the value of $x$ at which $f(x) = 2|x + 4|$ is not differentiable.

options.why: Read the corner straight off the $+4$ inside the modulus instead of solving $x + 4 = 0$.
Assumed every absolute value graph has its corner at the origin, ignoring the horizontal translation.
Divided the $-4$ by the coefficient $2$, treating the outside multiplier as a horizontal scale factor.

questions.solution_text:
$f(x) = \begin{cases} -2(x + 4), & x < -4 \\ 2(x + 4), & x \ge -4 \end{cases}$
For $x < -4$, $f'(x) = -2$
For $x > -4$, $f'(x) = 2$
The one-sided gradients differ, so there is a corner.
$f(x)$ is not differentiable at $x = -4$.

questions.question_text: Decide whether $f(x) = \begin{cases} x + 2, & x < -1 \\ x^{2} + 2, & x \ge -1 \end{cases}$ is differentiable at $x = -1$.

options.text: It is not differentiable at $x = -1$, because it is discontinuous there.
It is continuous but not differentiable at $x = -1$.
options.why: Notices the different gradients $1$ and $-2$ but incorrectly assumes the branch values $1$ and $3$ agree.

options.text: It is differentiable at $x = -1$, because each branch is a polynomial.
options.why: Checks the branches separately and ignores the jump at their join.

options.text: It is differentiable at $x = -1$, because $f(-1) = 3$ exists.
options.why: Treats a defined function value as sufficient for differentiability without checking continuity.

questions.solution_text:
Let $g(x) = x + 2$ and $h(x) = x^{2} + 2$
$g(-1) = -1 + 2 = 1$
$h(-1) = (-1)^{2} + 2 = 3$
The branch values differ, so $f(x)$ is discontinuous at $x = -1$.
A function cannot be differentiable where it is not continuous, so $f(x)$ is not differentiable at $x = -1$.

It is differentiable at $x = 2$, because the curve is smooth with no corner there.

As $x$ approaches $2$, the curve becomes steeper and steeper, so the tangent at $x = 2$ is vertical.

questions.question_text:
Consider $f(x) = \begin{cases} 2x + 1, & x < 0 \\ x^{2} + 1, & 0 \le x < 2 \\ 3x, & x \ge 2 \end{cases}$.
At which value or values of $x$ is $f(x)$ continuous but not differentiable?

options.text: $x = 0$ only
$x = 2$ only
options.why: Chose the join where the branch values disagree, so the function is not continuous there at all.
Counted every join where differentiability fails, without checking continuity separately at each one.

options.text: Neither, since $f(x)$ is differentiable at both joins
options.why: Checked only that each branch formula is differentiable, rather than comparing values and gradients at the joins.

questions.solution_text:
At $x = 0$:
$2(0) + 1 = 1$ and $0^{2} + 1 = 1$, so $f(x)$ is continuous.
The gradients are $2$ and $2(0) = 0$, which differ, so $f(x)$ is not differentiable at $x = 0$.
At $x = 2$:
$2^{2} + 1 = 5$ and $3(2) = 6$, so $f(x)$ is not continuous at $x = 2$.
$f(x)$ is continuous but not differentiable at $x = 0$ only.

questions.question_text: Decide whether $f(x) = \begin{cases} x^{3} - x, & x < -\dfrac{1}{2} \\ -\dfrac{1}{4}x + \dfrac{1}{4}, & x \ge -\dfrac{1}{2} \end{cases}$ is differentiable at $x = -\dfrac{1}{2}$.

options.text: It is differentiable there: both branch values are $\dfrac{3}{8}$ and both one-sided gradients are $-\dfrac{1}{4}$.
It is continuous but not differentiable there: the one-sided gradients are $-\dfrac{7}{4}$ and $-\dfrac{1}{4}$.
options.why: Treats $\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{2}$ as $-\dfrac{1}{4}$ when evaluating $3x^{2} - 1$.

options.text: It is not continuous there: the branch values are $-\dfrac{5}{8}$ and $\dfrac{3}{8}$.
options.why: Treats the term $-x$ as $-\dfrac{1}{2}$ rather than $\dfrac{1}{2}$ at $x = -\dfrac{1}{2}$.

options.text: It is continuous but not differentiable there, because a negative gradient cannot give a smooth join.
options.why: Mistakes a negative gradient for a failure of differentiability; equal finite negative gradients can give a smooth join.

questions.solution_text:
Let $g(x) = x^{3} - x$ and $h(x) = -\dfrac{1}{4}x + \dfrac{1}{4}$
$g\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = -\dfrac{1}{8} + \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{3}{8}$
$h\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \dfrac{1}{8} + \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{3}{8}$
The values agree, so $f(x)$ is continuous at $x = -\dfrac{1}{2}$.
$g'(x) = 3x^{2} - 1$, so $g'\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \dfrac{3}{4} - 1 = -\dfrac{1}{4}$
$h'(x) = -\dfrac{1}{4}$
The finite one-sided gradients agree, so $f(x)$ is differentiable at $x = -\dfrac{1}{2}$.

questions.question_text: For which of these functions is $x = 0$ a point where the function is continuous but not differentiable?

options.why: Confuses the cube root with the cube; $y = x^{3}$ is smooth at $x = 0$ and a horizontal tangent is not a failure.

questions.solution_text:
$f(x) = \sqrt[3]{x} = x^{\frac{1}{3}}$
$f(0) = 0$ and the curve passes through the origin with no break, so it is continuous at $x = 0$.
$f'(x) = \dfrac{1}{3}x^{-\frac{2}{3}}$
$= \dfrac{1}{3\sqrt[3]{x^{2}}}$
At $x = 0$ this is undefined, so the tangent there is vertical.
$f(x) = \sqrt[3]{x}$ is continuous but not differentiable at $x = 0$.
